papers.title: Idempotent generically stable measures in NSOP$_1$ groups
papers.label: arXiv:2611.31342v1

summary.one_liner: The paper proves the Idempotent Measure Conjecture for type-definable groups in NSOP$_1$ theories, showing that global idempotent generically stable (frequency interpretation) measures are unique left- and right-invariant measures concentrating on the type-definable stabilizer.
summary.plain:
This is a result in model theory, the branch of logic that studies which structures and definable sets behave well. The authors consider groups defined by logical formulas in a class of theories called NSOP$_1$ and show that a certain kind of "averaging" measure on such a group is essentially unique, and that its support has a simple algebraic structure. The argument also relies on an announced theorem by Ben Yaacov, Chernikov and Ramsey, whose proof is given in an appendix, to extend the conclusion to all such groups.</plain>
<parameter name="why">It settles a conjecture about how measures on definable groups behave in a broad class of theories, which bears on the structure theory of groups in model theory. Its wider connections are not spelled out in the text, so I cannot say more with confidence.
summary.background:
- Group: a set with an associative operation, identity and inverses; here the group is defined by logical formulas.
- Type-definable: described by a (possibly infinite) collection of logical conditions.
- Stabilizer: the subgroup of elements that preserve a given type under the group action.
- Measure (probability measure): an assignment of "sizes" or weights to definable sets, here used to average over the group.
- Left/right-invariant: unchanged when the group acts on the left or right.
- Idempotent: a measure that is equal to its own convolution (self-combination).
- NSOP$_1$: a dividing-independence property from stability-theory classification, a broad class of theories generalizing stable ones.
- Randomization: a construction that turns a theory into one about random variables/measures; the text cites a theorem that it preserves NSOP$_1$.
- Minimal left ideal and left-simple semigroup: standard algebraic notions from semigroup theory.

papers.abstract: We prove the Idempotent Measure Conjecture for type-definable groups in theories whose Keisler randomization is NSOP$_1$. More precisely, every global idempotent frequency interpretation measure on such a group is the unique left-invariant and the unique right-invariant measure concentrating on its type-definable stabilizer. In particular, its support is a left-simple convolution semigroup and has a unique minimal left ideal. The announced theorem of Ben Yaacov, Chernikov and Ramsey that randomization preserves NSOP$_1$ (proof in the appendix) yields the corresponding conclusion for all type-definable groups in NSOP$_1$ theories.

papers.title: Provability of Consistency: A New Foundational Landscape
papers.label: arXiv:2611.31591v1

summary.one_liner: A survey-style paper arguing that Hilbertian consistency of Peano Arithmetic, unlike the standard Gödelian consistency formula, can be proved inside PA itself, and claiming this refutes the Unprovability of Consistency Thesis.
summary.plain: The paper concerns a long-standing belief in logic: that a formal arithmetic system cannot prove, within itself, that it is free of contradictions. The authors claim that the usual formula for "consistency" used in Gödel's argument differs from the older, Hilbert-style notion, and that a proof of the older notion can be carried out inside the system. The text as given states this claim and summarizes its consequences but does not show the detailed proof.
summary.why: If correct, the claim would challenge a widely held result in the foundations of mathematics and bear on old philosophical arguments (such as the Lucas-Penrose argument about minds and machines) and on the design of self-checking theorem provers. The text alone does not let me judge whether the proof holds, and the claim is contested in its framing, so it should be read with that caution.
summary.background:
- Peano Arithmetic (PA): a standard formal system for the natural numbers and their basic arithmetic.
- Consistency: a theory is consistent if it never proves both a statement and its negation.
- Gödel's second incompleteness theorem: a consistent system of this strength cannot prove its own consistency formula, which is the basis of the "unprovability" thesis.
- Hilbert's consistency program: the early 20th-century aim to prove mathematics consistent using only safe, finitary methods.
- Gödelian vs. Hilbertian consistency: two different formal statements that both get called "consistency"; the paper's central claim is that they are not equivalent.
- Lucas-Penrose argument: a philosophical argument that human minds surpass any formal machine because machines cannot verify their own consistency.

papers.abstract: This paper surveys recent developments on the provability of consistency. For nearly a century, the Unprovability of Consistency Thesis (UCT) has held that sufficiently rich systems, such as Peano Arithmetic (PA), cannot formalize a proof of their own consistency. Recent studies show that the standard G\"odelian consistency formula, Con_PA, on which the UCT argument rests, represents a non-equivalent redefinition of the original Hilbertian notion of consistency. We construct a rigorous mathematical proof of the Hilbertian consistency of PA that is formalizable within PA itself, thereby refuting UCT. While G\"odelian consistency formulas remain indispensable for comparing the relative strengths of theories, Hilbertian consistency enables internal self-verification. Beyond vindicating Hilbert's consistency program, these findings dismantle the Lucas-Penrose argument and remove perceived logical barriers to self-verifying Automated Theorem Proving and Artificial Intelligence.

papers.title: Cardinal Transfer Events for Infinitary Logic with Infinitary Quantification
papers.label: arXiv:2611.31725v1

summary.background:
- Infinitary logic: logical languages that allow infinitely long conjunctions or disjunctions, unlike ordinary finite formulas.
- Infinitary quantification: quantifiers ("for all", "there exists") ranging over infinitely many objects at once, not just finitely many.
- Cardinals: measures of infinite size, such as how many elements an infinite set has.
- Predicates: properties or relations that a logical formula can express about objects.
- Transfer event (cardinal transfer): a statement that a structure with one pair of infinite sizes has a substructure with another pair, a standard tool in model theory.
- Gap-n problem: a question about whether certain cardinal transfer properties hold at a given level of complexity; the abstract does not define it further.
- Assumed theory Φ: an extra hypothesis, not identified in the text, on which the results depend.
summary.one_liner: Under the assumption of a certain theory Φ, the paper claims to solve the Gap-n problem for more than one predicate in infinitary logic with infinitary quantification, via cardinal transfer events.
summary.plain: This paper is about a question in the foundations of mathematics: when a logical language can talk about very large infinite sizes (cardinals), and whether certain "transfer" properties of those sizes hold. The text is only a short abstract. It says the authors solve a version of the "Gap-n problem" for more than one predicate, but only under an extra assumption they call the theory Φ.
summary.why: The abstract is too brief to show how strong the result is or which open questions it settles, so its importance is hard to judge from this text alone. It likely matters to specialists in infinitary logic and set theory, but the connection to wider mathematics is not stated.

papers.abstract: Assuming the existence of a certain theory $\Phi$, we solve the Gap-$n$ problem for more than one predicate. This will be done for infinitary logic with infinitary quantification.

papers.title: Alpha-Beta Pruning via Monadic Continuations
papers.label: arXiv:2611.32320v1

summary.background:
- Minimax: a search method where one player maximises and the opponent minimises the final score, looking ahead through possible moves.
- Alpha-beta pruning: an optimisation of minimax that skips branches which cannot affect the final decision.
- Monad: a programming abstraction for chaining computations with extra context (here, the continuation and reader monads manage control flow and passed-in bounds).
- Continuation: a way of representing "what happens next" as a function, letting a search decide when to stop early.
- Formal correctness proof: a mathematical argument that the optimised method always gives the same answer as the simple one.
summary.one_liner: The paper gives a monadic (continuation- and reader-monad based) formulation of alpha-beta pruning for minimax game search, records bounds inside outcomes rather than move types, extends the ordinary continuation monad to return optimal plays, and proves the pruned search agrees with exhaustive minimax.
summary.plain: The paper looks at a classic method that lets a game-playing program skip parts of its search tree when those parts cannot change the best move. The authors rewrite this method using a programming pattern called monads, which packages computations in a structured way. They show it finds the same best outcomes and best sequences of moves as checking every option, and they test it on Tic-Tac-Toe, where it evaluated 39 times fewer plays than exhaustive search.
summary.why: It offers a compositional, formally verified way to express a foundational AI search algorithm inside functional programming, which may matter for building and checking game-playing software. The text reports only a single Tic-Tac-Toe test, so how well the approach scales to larger games is not shown here.

papers.abstract: Alpha-beta pruning is a fundamental technique in game-playing AI, enabling efficient minimax search by avoiding the exploration of branches that cannot affect the optimal decision. We present a monadic formulation of alpha-beta pruning based on the combination of the continuation monad and the reader monad. Unlike previous approaches that encode alpha-beta bounds into the types of available moves, our construction records these bounds within monadic outcomes, leaving the move types unchanged. We further show that the ordinary continuation monad suffices to compute not only optimal outcomes but also optimal plays, by extending the outcome type to include the corresponding sequences of moves. This provides an alternative to generalisations of the continuation monad proposed to address the inefficiencies associated with the selection monad in alpha-beta search. We illustrate our approach with an implementation of Tic-Tac-Toe, observing a 39-fold reduction in the number of plays evaluated, compared with exhaustive search, in computing an optimal play. Finally, we formally establish the correctness of our construction by proving that the monadic alpha-beta search computes the same optimal outcomes and plays as exhaustive minimax search. Our results demonstrate how a foundational algorithm in AI can be expressed and verified using standard monadic abstractions, providing a basis for further development of compositional approaches to adversarial search.

papers.title: $\Sigma^1_3$ Gandy-Harrington Forcing
papers.label: arXiv:2611.29432v1

summary.background:
- Descriptive set theory: the study of definable sets of reals (infinite binary sequences) and their complexity, organised in the projective hierarchy (Σ, Π, Δ levels).
- Forcing: a technique for building new models of set theory by adding generic objects; Gandy-Harrington forcing is a specific forcing that builds sets with prescribed definability.
- Silver's dichotomy: a theorem saying that analytic equivalence relations have either countably many classes or a perfect set of inequivalent elements; Harrington's proof used this forcing.
- Determinacy: the assertion that certain two-player infinite games have a winning strategy for one player; its strength is measured by level in the projective hierarchy.
- Reverse mathematics: determining which axioms are logically necessary to prove a given theorem.
- Inner models and basis theorems: results saying that definable sets have members constructible in a suitable inner model (a restricted universe of sets).
summary.one_liner: The paper builds a higher-level version of Gandy-Harrington forcing for the projective hierarchy under a local determinacy hypothesis, and uses it for a reverse mathematics result at the Δ^1_2-Determinacy level and an inner-model basis theorem for Σ^1_3 sets.
summary.plain: This is a paper in mathematical logic about the structure of "definable" sets of infinite sequences of whole numbers, which are the objects studied in descriptive set theory. The authors adapt a known proof technique, Gandy-Harrington forcing, to a more complex level of that hierarchy. The text says this new version lets them prove a result about which axioms are needed for certain determinacy statements, and a new basis theorem for a class of sets.
summary.why: The abstract points to two concrete outcomes: a reverse mathematics result (identifying the exact axioms needed for a statement) and a basis theorem for Σ^1_3 sets. Its significance rests on how well the new forcing generalises, which the short text does not show; the connections to wider logic are the authors' claims and I have not checked them.

papers.abstract: Gandy-Harrington forcing is an important tool in descriptive set theory, first developed by Gandy and later used by Harrington to give a simple proof of Silver's dichotomy theorem. In this paper, we develop a new version of Gandy-Harrington forcing higher up in the projective hierarchy, under an appropriate local determinacy hypothesis. Using this new forcing, we prove a reverse mathematics result at the level of $\Delta^1_2$-Determinacy as well as new inner-model-theoretic basis theorem for $\Sigma^1_3$ sets.

papers.title: On Cohen Generic Sets in Supercompact Prikry Extensions
papers.label: arXiv:2611.30821v1

summary.background:
- Forcing: a method for adding new sets to a model of set theory, using a partially ordered set of finite approximations.
- Cardinals and cofinality: the size of infinite sets and the length of cofinal sequences; "singular" cardinals are those that are not regular.
- Large cardinals: κ being λ-supercompact is a strong infinity axiom about embeddings of the universe; it is a very strong consequence of set theory.
- Prikry-type forcing: a forcing that changes the cofinality of a measurable-type cardinal without collapsing cardinals.
- Projection: a map between forcings that preserves generic extensions, so one forcing is essentially a quotient of another.
- Diamond principle (◇) on stationary sets: a combinatorial guessing principle that holds in some models and fails in others.
- Strategic closure and distributivity: closure properties of forcings that limit the new sets they add.
- Independence: a statement neither provable nor refutable from the standard axioms.
summary.one_liner: Under a supercompactness assumption on κ and a diamond-type principle on stationary subsets of λ, the paper shows that small strategically closed forcings are projections of λ-supercompact Prikry forcing, and it studies limits on κ-distributive projections, including size-λ examples that fail to be projections.
summary.plain: This is set theory work on the forcing method, a way of extending the universe of sets by adding new objects. The paper asks which kinds of forcing notions can be reproduced, in a precise "projection" sense, by one particular forcing called supercompact Prikry forcing. The text reports that, under a set-theoretic guessing principle and a cardinal-size condition, the answer is yes for a broad class, while in some other cases the answer is shown to be independent of the usual axioms, and some specific examples are shown not to fit.
summary.why: It maps which forcing notions can be realized inside a single canonical model-building tool, which clarifies the structure of large-cardinal forcing extensions. The abstract gives no wider applications, so its significance beyond this area is unclear from the text alone.

papers.abstract: Let $\kappa$ be $\lambda$-supercompact for a regular $\lambda>\kappa$. We show that if $\lambda$ is not the successor of a singular of cofinality below $\kappa$, $\diamondsuit(S^\lambda_{\geq\kappa})$ implies that every ${<}\kappa$-strategically closed forcing of size at most $\lambda$ is a projection of the $\lambda$-supercompact Prikry forcing. We show that the situation for successors of singulars of small cofinality is independent. Finally, we provide more limitations about the class of $\kappa$-distributive projections of the $\lambda$-supercompact Prikry forcing and give examples of $\kappa$-distributive forcings of size $\lambda$ which cannot be projections of this forcing.

papers.title: Bridging Badiou's Gaps: Topos Theory and the Bodies of Mathematical Expression
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27280v1

summary.background:
- Badiou: a French philosopher whose works Being and Event and Logics of Worlds use set theory and topos theory to describe truth, events and change.
- Topos (plural topoi): a mathematical structure from category theory that generalises set theory and can serve as a setting for logic.
- Category theory: a framework that studies mathematical objects through the relationships (maps) between them rather than their internal contents.
- Forcing: Paul Cohen's technique for building new models of set theory, used to show certain statements cannot be proved or disproved from the standard axioms.
- Kripke-Joyal semantics: a way of giving meaning to logical statements inside a topos.
- Localic: a more restricted, point-based form of topos, which the author argues Badiou relied on.
- Grothendieck topos: a general notion of topos introduced in algebraic geometry.
- Johnstone's "universe of discourse": a description of a topos as a setting in which mathematical reasoning takes place.
summary.one_liner: A philosophical reconstruction of Alain Badiou's use of topos theory (forcing, Kripke-Joyal semantics, and his typology of change) recast in a categorical framework, arguing that a topos can be read as a "body of mathematical expression."
summary.plain: The paper revisits how the philosopher Alain Badiou used a branch of advanced mathematics, topos theory, in his books Being and Event and Logics of Worlds. The author argues that Badiou shrank this mathematics down to a narrow, set-based version, and asks what is lost when it is restored to its fuller categorical form. The author says the aim is conceptual clarification rather than new mathematical results.
summary.why: It connects philosophy of mathematics, the foundations of logic, and the reception of category theory in continental philosophy, and it is a second part of an argument begun in 2013. The text itself does not show how much influence the argument has, so its wider significance is uncertain.

papers.abstract: This article develops a second stage of an argument begun in 2013, revisiting Alain Badiou's use of topos theory in Being and Event and Logics of Worlds. The previous article diagnosed Badiou's reduction of topos theory to its atomistic, localic form as the scientific scapegoat in his attack on 'democratic materialism'. Now I ask what follows when this logicist illusion is dispelled and the categorical alternative is taken seriously, particularly with respect to forcing, semantic expression, and mathematical subjectification that constitute the key elements of Badiou's earlier work. I thus reconstruct Badiou's own arguments in a corrected form, while transferring them to a categorical framework. The aim is not to introduce new mathematical results, but to identify what is conceptually lost through their reduction to set-theoretic formalism. In particular, I describe Cohen's forcing argument in the context of Grothendieck topoi and Kripke-Joyal semantics, thereby explicating the geometric structures implicit in Badiou's thinking. This reconstruction further brings into view a different way of understanding Badiou's concepts of subject, body, and change. Rather than treating a topos as merely a formal container for mathematical objects, I propose reading it as a body of mathematical expression, aligning with Johnstone's characterization of a topos as a 'universe of discourse'. At the same time, the geometrization of logic allows Badiou's own four-fold typology of change - when applied to topos theory itself as a mathematical 'event' - to be anchored to various historical definitions of a topos. In this way, the article bridges Badiou's two major works while clarifying how his own limited expression of mathematical formalism embodies his 'dialectical', ultimately singular concept of the event, and the way it clouds his philosophical understanding of locality and temporality.

papers.title: The Power Of Enumerations
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27239v1

summary.background:
- Computability theory asks which infinite sets of numbers can be computed from which others.
- Turing degree: a class of sets that are equally hard to compute from one another, under ordinary Turing computation.
- Enumeration degree: a coarser-to-finer notion where a set is computed by listing its members (positive information only), not by deciding membership.
- Generic and random sets: "typical" infinite sets that avoid all definable special properties (genericity) or are incompressible/unpredictable (randomness). Levels (2-generic, 3-generic, 1-random, weak 2-random) measure how strongly typical.
- Quasiminimal: an enumeration degree with no non-computable (total) degrees strictly below it, apart from trivial ones.
- PA degrees: degrees that compute a solution to a certain combinatorial principle (Peano arithmetic-related), and dimension 1 sets are a measure of how much of the set's information is free.
summary.one_liner: The paper studies the computational strength of enumeration reducibility for generic and random sets, showing limits on what enumerations of 3-generics and weak 2-randoms can compute and mapping which Turing degrees can lie above quasiminimal enumeration degrees.
summary.plain:
The paper is about how much information can be extracted from "typical" infinite sets of binary digits, using a way of computing called enumeration, which asks whether a set can be listed out from another set rather than decided item by item. The authors show that some such listing-based constructions cannot recover typical sets at higher levels of typicality. They also answer an open question of Slaman and Sorbi by showing that some quasiminimal degrees have no minimal Turing degrees above them.</plain>
<parameter name="why">It sharpens the picture of how randomness and genericity behave under computability reductions, a central topic in the study of what can be computed from what. The text itself does not say how these results bear on wider applications, so their broader significance is unclear from this text alone.

papers.abstract: We study the computational strength of enumerations of generic and random sets, particularly its interplay with computing these `typical' sets. We show that, while enumerations of $2$-generics can compute $2$-generics, this fails at higher levels---every $3$-generic has an enumeration which computes no weak $3$-generic. The analogous statement holds for randoms---every weak $2$-random has an enumeration which computes no $1$-random. We then analyze the total degrees above a quasiminimal enumeration degree, showing certain restrictions as well as certain positive results on the possible Turing degrees in such a cone. This answers a question of Slaman and Sorbi, by showing that there are quasiminimals with no minimal Turing degrees above them. We also show that while every total degree above some quasiminimals compute dimension $1$ sets, the total degrees above any quasiminimal fail to be a subset of the PA degrees.

papers.title: Invariance and Expressiveness: Modal Variations
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26244v1

summary.background:
- Modal logic: a logic with "necessarily" and "possibly" operators, read over graphs of states and transitions (Kripke structures).
- Bisimulation: a back-and-forth matching between two state graphs such that matched states agree on their local facts and can mirror each other's moves; the two are then indistinguishable in the logic.
- Bisimulation invariance: a property of a formula or query whose truth is unchanged by such matchings.
- Expressive completeness: the claim that a logic can define every property of a given kind that has the relevant invariance.
- van Benthem–Rosen characterisation: the theorem that, on finite structures, modal logic is exactly the bisimulation-invariant fragment of first-order logic.
- Lindström theorem: a result saying a logic is maximal among logics satisfying certain abstract criteria.
- Finite model theory: the study of logic restricted to finite structures, where many standard tools fail.
summary.one_liner: A survey-style overview of bisimulation invariance in modal logic, covering variant bisimulation notions, matching modalities beyond Kripke structures, and expressive completeness results in the style of van Benthem–Rosen and Lindström theorems.
summary.plain: This is a survey-style paper about when a formal language for describing systems (modal logic) can only tell apart situations that are "the same" under a particular kind of matching between them, called bisimulation. It reviews classical results and newer extensions, including variants of that matching and settings where the usual tools of finite model theory are hard to apply. The main theme is expressive completeness: showing that a logic captures exactly the properties that respect this matching, and that it is maximal in a suitable sense.
summary.why: The text is an abstract-level description, so the specific results are not shown here. It may matter to researchers in logic and computer science who use modal logic to model systems, since expressiveness limits tell you what a language can and cannot say about them.

papers.abstract: This contribution focuses on bisimulation invariance as the hallmark of modal model theory and of modal modelling. It exemplifies traditional as well as more recent ramifications \&\ extensions of classical results -- involving variant modes of bisimulation equivalence and matching modalities also beyond plain Kripke structures, and emphasising especially the technical challenges in finite model theory and other non-elementary settings. Main results to be discussed revolve about the theme of expressive completeness phenomena: beside expressive completeness under bisimulation invariance in relation to first-order background logics, in the style of van Benthem--Rosen characterisations, this also concerns maximality results under criteria form abstract model theory, in the style of Lindstroem theorems.

papers.title: Computational trust as intuitionistic knowledge
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25799v1

summary.background:
- Intuitionistic logic: a version of logic in which a claim counts as known only when you have a constructive proof of it, not merely because its denial leads to contradiction.
- Modal logic: an extension of ordinary logic with operators such as "it is necessary that" or, here, "one trusts that."
- Proofs-as-programs correspondence: the idea that a formal proof can be read as a program, and a program as a proof of its specification.
- Verification: checking, by formal reasoning or testing, that a program meets its specification.
- Fallible knowledge: knowledge that can turn out to be false, unlike infallible knowledge.
summary.one_liner: The paper argues that computational trust can be modeled as fallible intuitionistic knowledge grounded in verification, and gives a simple constructive modal logic with a trust modality, specified inferentially via proofs-as-programs.
summary.plain: The paper asks what it means to trust a computer program. Its answer is that trust can be treated as a kind of knowledge that rests on having verified the program, but that is open to being wrong. The authors build a small formal logic to capture this idea.
summary.why: The logic is designed so that verification leads to trust, but trust does not automatically lead to verification, which matches the everyday idea that one can rely on a program on good grounds and still be let down. The abstract does not say how this connects to practical software assurance or other applications, so that link is unclear from the text.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we will argue that the notion of computational trust can be understood as a form of fallible intuitionistic knowledge grounded in verification. This approach naturally captures a key aspect of trust: it involves vulnerability. Specifically, it validates the principle that verification leads to trust but does not validate the opposite principle that trust leads to verification. Thus, we can trust on good grounds that some program will perform according to its specification but the program might still fail. We present a simple logic for capturing this notion of computational trust based on constructive modal propositional logic extended with a trust modality, which will be specified in an inferential fashion and by utilizing the proofs-as-programs correspondence.

papers.title: Preserving Ramsey ultrafilters with tree forcings
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23713v1

summary.background:
- Cardinal characteristics: numerical invariants measuring the size of infinite collections, such as the dominating number d and the ultrafilter number u.
- ZFC: the standard axioms of set theory (Zermelo-Fraenkel with Choice); a consistency result shows a statement cannot be ruled out from these axioms.
- Forcing: a technique for extending a model of set theory by adding new sets, used to build models where chosen statements hold.
- Ultrafilter: a maximal family of subsets of the natural numbers that is closed under finite intersections and supersets; a Ramsey ultrafilter is a special, well-behaved kind.
- Preservation: showing a forcing extension keeps a given ultrafilter from being destroyed, which controls how cardinals relate.
- Aleph notation: aleph_1 and aleph_2 denote the first and second infinite cardinals.
summary.one_liner: The paper defines normed-tree forcings, a broad class of tree-shaped set-theoretic forcing notions (including fat-tree forcings), shows they can preserve Ramsey ultrafilters, and uses this to establish the ZFC consistency of d = u = aleph_1 < minLc = c = aleph_2.
summary.plain: This is a paper in set theory, the branch of mathematics that studies infinity and its different sizes. The authors study a family of ways of enlarging the universe of sets, built from tree-shaped structures, and show that these enlargements keep a special kind of large collection of sets (a Ramsey ultrafilter) intact. They use this to show that a certain arrangement of infinite sizes of several mathematical quantities is consistent with the standard axioms.
summary.why: The work settles open questions about how several classical cardinal characteristics relate to one another, in particular whether the ultrafilter number can be strictly smaller than certain localization and evasion-type cardinals. The text does not indicate further applications beyond these relations, so its wider significance is best judged by specialists.

papers.abstract: We define a wide class of tree forcings that we call $\textit{normed-tree forcings}$ and prove that they can preserve Ramsey ultrafilters. These include $\textit{fat-tree forcings}$ as particular cases. As an application, we prove the consistency with $\mathsf{ZFC}$ of $\mathfrak{d}=\mathfrak{u}=\aleph_1 < \mathsf{minLc}=\mathfrak{c}=\aleph_2$, where $\mathfrak{d}$ denotes the dominating number, $\mathfrak{u}$ the ultrafilter number, and $\mathsf{minLc}$ the minimum localization cardinal. This solves some open questions about pairs of classical cardinal characteristics, such as the consistency of both $\mathfrak{e}_{\mathsf{ubd}}$ and its dual strictly larger than $\mathfrak{u}$.

papers.title: Proof Checking Continuous Reachability
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25303v1

summary.background:
- Ordinary differential equations (ODEs): equations describing how quantities change continuously over time.
- Reachability: determining which states a system can reach from a set of starting states.
- Taylor models: a way of representing a function as a polynomial plus a rigorously bounded error term, giving guaranteed bounds on numerical answers.
- Polynomial vector fields: rules of change where the rates are polynomial expressions in the variables.
- Differential dynamic logic (dL): a formal logic for stating and proving properties of hybrid systems, with KeYmaera X as its prover.
- Proof checking: independently re-verifying a proof produced by a solver, so the solver need not be trusted; the SAT/UNSAT proof analogy is the model here.
- Lean 4: a proof assistant and programming language used to implement the checker.
- ARCH competition: a community benchmark contest for verifying continuous and hybrid systems.
summary.one_liner: The paper introduces a proof format and a Lean 4 proof checker that certify Taylor-model reachability computations for ODEs with polynomial vector fields, expressed as proofs in differential dynamic logic (dL) and checkable in KeYmaera X, and proves that such proofs can be generated whenever a correct approximation exists.
summary.plain: Computer programs that predict where a system governed by continuous change (such as a moving machine or physical process) will end up often use numerical approximations that can be wrong without anyone noticing. This paper designs a way for such a program to output a formal proof of its answer, and a separate checker that verifies that proof. The authors show that if an approximation was computed correctly, a matching proof can always be generated and checked, and they report that the checker verifies benchmarks from the ARCH competition.
summary.why: Certifying results from untrusted numerical software matters for safety verification of cyber-physical systems, where a wrong prediction could hide a dangerous state. The approach is modeled on proof checking for SAT solvers, which is a useful precedent, though the text alone does not show how widely it will be adopted.

papers.abstract: This paper introduces a proof format and proof checker for certifying reachability computations of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) with polynomial vector fields. Establishing a proof checking framework for certifying ODE reachability is similar to the checking of UNSAT proofs for propositional satisfiability solving, but it is even more important due to the challenges inherent in dealing with ODEs, and even more challenging due to the numerical nature of ODE reachability algorithms. The proofs are expressed in differential dynamic logic (dL), and can be independently verified with symbolic theorem provers for dL (e.g. KeYmaeraX). Such proofs are naturally generated by reachability algorithms based on Taylor models, a popular technique to obtain rigorous bounds on approximations of ODEs. This paper proves the completeness of such proofs - if an approximation was correctly computed by some (possibly untrusted) reachability algorithm via Taylor models, then a corresponding proof in dL can be automatically generated and checked to be correct in dL's proof calculus. A dedicated proof checker is implemented in Lean4 for improved performance, which is capable of formally verifying benchmarks in the ARCH competition.

papers.title: Relative computability and definability for nonregular oracles
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22871v1

summary.background:
- Computable set: one where a procedure can decide membership for any input.
- Computably enumerable (c.e.): one whose members can be listed by a procedure, though non-members may never be confirmed.
- Oracle: extra information handed to a procedure for free; "relative to X" means computing with X as the oracle.
- Turing reducibility: A is Turing reducible to X if X-powered procedures can decide A.
- Pointwise vs. strong reducibility: two variants of the reduction notion that can differ.
- Nonstandard model of arithmetic: a model of the arithmetic truths that contains extra, non-standard numbers; true arithmetic is the set of all sentences true in the standard integers.
- ISigma_1: a fragment of induction axioms restricted to simple formulas, used to say how much arithmetic is assumed.
- Delta_1 set: one that is both c.e. and co-c.e. (so decidable in the simple sense).
summary.one_liner: In nonstandard models of true arithmetic, the classical equivalence between computability and "both the set and its complement are c.e. relative to an oracle" is shown to fail for general (nonregular) oracles, with the regular case still holding over ISigma_1.
summary.plain: This paper works in logic about what can be computed from a given body of information (an "oracle"). The authors build a countable nonstandard model of arithmetic in which a set A and its complement can both be listed by a procedure using oracle X, yet A cannot be obtained from X by a standard step-by-step reduction. The result is a counterexample, and the authors also prove that the usual equivalence does hold for regular oracles.
summary.why: It shows that a classical equivalence in computability theory depends on the kind of oracle used, which clarifies the boundaries of a basic principle. The text does not say what further applications it may have, so its wider connections are unclear from the given material.

papers.abstract: Classically, a set is computable from an oracle if both the set and its complement are computably enumerable (c.e.) relative to that oracle. We construct a countable nonstandard model of true arithmetic with sets A and X such that both A and its complement are c.e. relative to X, yet A is not pointwise Turing reducible to X. The Turing functionals used here are single-valued at every oracle. For regular oracles, we prove that the classical equivalence holds over ISigma_1. Two further phenomena, each known from earlier work, are realized with the same oracle X that witnesses our main separation. Strong and pointwise Turing reducibility differ for this X, and some Delta_1^X set is not X-c.e.

papers.title: Exactly Proper Forcing
papers.label: arXiv:2611.21390v1

summary.background:
- Set theory: the foundation of mathematics built on sets, with the axioms of ZFC as the usual standard.
- Forcing: a technique for extending a model of set theory by adding new sets, used to show that statements are independent of the axioms.
- Properness: a property of forcing notions that ensures countable structures are preserved, allowing iterated constructions.
- Uncountable models: models whose underlying collection is larger than the natural numbers, where properness alone may not suffice.
- Forcing axioms: strong consistency principles (such as Martin's Axiom or Proper Forcing Axiom) asserting that certain forcing extensions already contain the needed objects.
- Iteration theorem: a result saying that a sequence of such forcings, taken in stages, still has the desired property.
summary.one_liner: Introduces "exact properness," a strengthened form of properness for forcing over uncountable models of set theory, proves iteration theorems, and shows consistency of forcing axioms for this class.
summary.plain: This paper is about a technical tool in set theory, the branch of mathematics that studies infinity and what can and cannot be proved about it. Set theorists build new mathematical universes by "forcing," a method for adding objects to a model while controlling what changes. The author introduces a stricter version of a known safety condition, called exact properness, and shows that the approach works when applied repeatedly and that certain general principles, called forcing axioms, can be consistently assumed for this class.
summary.why: Forcing axioms are central tools for settling questions that the standard axioms of set theory leave open, so a new class of well-behaved forcings that supports them may matter to specialists. The text is short and gives only the abstract, so I cannot judge how far the results reach beyond what is stated.

papers.abstract: We introduce the notion of exact properness, a strong form of properness for uncountable models, and prove iteration theorems and the consistency of forcing axioms for this class. We discuss examples of posets in the class and give some applications of the forcing axioms.

papers.title: On cover exacting cardinals
papers.label: arXiv:2611.20299v1

summary.background:
- Cardinals: infinite "sizes" of sets; large cardinals are very big ones whose existence cannot be proved from the standard axioms of set theory.
- Strongly compact cardinal: a large cardinal with a strong covering property for families of sets; ω_1-strongly compact is a weaker, countably-complete version of this.
- Cover exacting (γ-cover exacting): a property of a cardinal λ relative to a cardinal γ, defined in the literature the paper cites; the excerpt does not define it.
- Open question of Goldberg: the paper responds to a question in Goldberg's earlier work, which the excerpt does not describe.
- Background in forcing or inner-model theory is helpful but not needed for the headline claim.
summary.one_liner: The paper answers a question of Goldberg by showing that, if κ is ω_1-strongly compact, no cardinal λ > κ is γ-cover exacting for any cardinal γ.
summary.plain: This is a set-theory paper about very large infinite numbers called cardinals, which are used to measure how strong the basic axioms of mathematics can be. The author answers an open question posed by Goldberg about a particular large-cardinal property called "cover exacting." The result shows that a certain kind of large cardinal (an ω_1-strongly compact one) rules out any larger cardinal having that property.
summary.why: It settles a specific open question raised by another researcher, which narrows down which large-cardinal properties can coexist. The text itself does not say how far the result reaches beyond this question, so its wider significance is unclear from the excerpt alone.

papers.abstract: We answer a question of Goldberg about cover exacting cardinals. Concretely, we show that if $κ$ is $ω_1$-strongly compact, then no cardinal $λ>κ$ is $γ$-cover exacting for some cardinal $γ$.
